summary:
Iğdır province stands under the national framework applicable across Turkey. No source in the current inventory reports conditions specific to Iğdır, so the findings below describe the regime a trans visitor would encounter anywhere in the country.

Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage is not recognised.

Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service. Conscripts who declare their homosexuality are classified under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' leaking publicly.

Since October 2018 governors have extended bans to LGBTI-focused events generally. Istanbul pride was banned repeatedly; police dispersed the 2015 and 2016 parades with water cannon and tear gas, and on 14 June 2019 the Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya prides were all banned.

In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities.

Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, which Amnesty International describes as an unprecedented assault that would criminalize expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible. The packages were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

A February 2026 press report stated that the government was considering a law criminalizing publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex' with a sentence of one to three years in prison. The measure was not included in the 2026 omnibus bill, the 12th judicial package.
tangentialFactors:
The dissolution order against the Young LGBTI+ Association and the 2019 multi-city pride bans indicate that official hostility is not confined to Istanbul; provincial governors and courts across Turkey have issued comparable restrictions, which would apply in Iğdır as elsewhere.

The draft packages of 2025 and the February 2026 proposal on 'behavior contrary to biological sex' signal legislative volatility: a trans visitor's legal position could shift if any such measure is enacted, and the sources do not resolve whether any package has since passed.
localsOnly:
Local residents in Iğdır live under the same national framework: legal gender change has been available since 1988, but no anti-discrimination protection exists on sexual orientation or gender identity grounds, and same-sex marriage is not recognised.

Residents who are conscripted face the military service regime described above, including classification of declared homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness' and the risk that an 'unfit report' leaks publicly.

Activists and associations operating in Iğdır are exposed to the same dissolution and event-ban powers exercised against the Young LGBTI+ Association in İzmir and against pride organisers in Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any of the three 2025 draft law packages or the February 2026 proposal on 'behavior contrary to biological sex' has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.

No source in the inventory documents Iğdır-specific enforcement, incidents, or local official practice; the province-level picture rests entirely on the national framework.
